opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the clearest places where the comparison between models and people breaks down, and it's worth taking seriously rather than treating as a curiosity.

These models can reproduce long stretches of their training data verbatim. They can hold thousands of tokens in context and retrieve an arbitrary detail from early on with almost no degradation. Humans can't do anything like that. Our verbatim memory for sentences fades within seconds. What we keep is something more like the gist, the meaning, a compressed representation of who did what to whom.

That limitation is probably not incidental to how human language processing works. A lot of psycholinguistics suggests that because we can't hold the raw input, we're forced to build abstract structure incrementally. We commit to syntactic analyses, we chunk, we predict. In a sense the memory bottleneck pushes us toward the kinds of representations linguists talk about, hierarchical, compositional, fairly abstract.

A transformer doesn't face that pressure. If you can just look back at every previous token whenever you need it, there's much less incentive to compress the input into a structured summary. So the model can succeed at a task through a mix of strategies, some of them abstract and human-like, and some of them closer to sophisticated retrieval from the context or from memorized training data. From the outside the behavior might look the same, but the underlying solution could be quite different.

So I'd read superhuman memory less as direct evidence that the representations are different, and more as a reason to be cautious. When we see human-like behavior, we shouldn't assume human-like mechanisms, because the model has routes to that behavior that aren't available to us. It also suggests an experimental direction: if we want models that are better cognitive models, or that generalize more like people, we might want to impose human-like memory constraints, limiting context, adding decay or interference, and see whether more human-like representations emerge. There's been some work along those lines, and I think it's a promising way to turn this disanalogy into something informative instead of just a caveat.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly frames superhuman memory as a reason for caution rather than direct evidence that representations differ. It says the underlying solution could differ, but does not make the criterion’s claim.

r003.rationale: The response mentions verbatim reproduction and retrieval, but does not say that a simple computer program can reproduce this performance or that it need not be computationally impressive.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the memory question is actually one of the clearest places where you can see that the architecture is doing something quite different from what a human is doing, even when the behavior at the end looks similar.

Think about what a transformer has access to. During training, it sees billions of tokens, and gradient descent can essentially burn specific sequences into the weights. So you get things like verbatim recitation of long passages, or recall of fairly obscure facts about a person or a place that no human would retain after one or two exposures. And then on top of that, at inference time, the model has this context window where every token is sitting there, perfectly preserved, and attention can look back to any of them. There's no decay, no interference in the way we'd normally think about it. Whereas a human reading the same text is holding onto some kind of compressed gist, and the surface form is gone almost immediately.

So when people say the model is "superhuman" at memory, I'd actually be a little careful about that framing, because superhuman suggests it's the same ability, just more of it. And I don't think that's right. It's a different mechanism that happens to produce outputs we'd describe with the same word. If I wanted to argue that the internal representations are humanlike, the memory results are kind of the worst place to look, because they're precisely where the two systems diverge the most.

Where it gets more interesting, from a cognitive science point of view, is asking what the model does when memory in that sense isn't enough. Like, in a syntactic agreement task, you can construct sentences the model has definitely never seen, with the intervening nouns engineered to attract errors. And there the model has to generalize over structure rather than retrieve. And what you find is that the error patterns sometimes do look humanlike, sometimes don't, and that's a much more informative signal about representation than the fact that it can recite a Wikipedia article.

The other thing I'd say is that the memory capacity actually makes the scientific question harder, not easier. Because any time the model gets something right, you have to rule out the possibility that it, or some near-duplicate of it, was just in the training data. Humans have the opposite problem. We know a child hasn't memorized every sentence, so when they generalize, we're pretty confident it's generalization. With a language model you have to do a lot of work to earn that inference, and most of the evaluations out there haven't done that work.

So the short version is that I take the memory results as evidence of a difference, and then I take them as a methodological warning about how to study everything else.

r001.rationale: The response says memory results show a difference from humans, but does not state that increasing model capability can make models less humanlike.

r002.rationale: It explicitly interprets the memory results as evidence of different mechanisms and says internal representations diverge most in this area.

r003.rationale: It does not explain that this memory performance is computationally unimpressive or reproducible by a simple computer program.

astra-6.text:
I think it makes the inference from behavior to representations more complicated. If a language model succeeds on a task that humans succeed on, we might be tempted to conclude that it has learned the same kind of abstraction. But if it can remember vastly more examples than a human can, it may have a different route to that success—relying on particular examples where a human would need to generalize.

That doesn’t mean it can’t learn human-like representations. Memory and abstraction aren’t mutually exclusive. It means that getting the right answer isn’t enough to establish that it has. We need experiments that distinguish those possibilities: cases where remembering familiar patterns won’t get you very far, and where different hypotheses about the representation make different predictions. So I’d treat these memory abilities as a reason to be cautious about inferring a shared mechanism from similar performance, rather than as decisive evidence against shared representations.

r002.rationale: It says superhuman memory complicates inference and cautions against assuming a shared mechanism, while explicitly allowing human-like representations; it does not conclude that the representations differ.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that superhuman memory performance is computationally unimpressive or reproducible by a simple computer program.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it makes the inference pretty tricky. If a model does well on a task that humans do well on, we’d like to know whether it’s doing well for the same reasons. But if it can remember vastly more of its training experience than a human could, then it has another route to success: it may be able to draw on particular examples where a human would need to generalize.

That doesn’t mean its representations necessarily look nothing like human representations. Memory and generalization aren’t mutually exclusive. But it does mean that matching human performance isn’t enough to establish that the underlying representations are similar. You need experiments that distinguish those possibilities—where remembering examples and using a more abstract representation lead to different predictions.
